findings.summary: The lazy import inside is_expandable executes a `from .pretty import` statement on every invocation instead of once, adding per-call overhead in a hot rendering loop.
findings.failure_scenario: When _collect_renderables processes an iterable containing many non-str/non-Text/non-ConsoleRenderable objects, is_expandable is called once per object, and each call runs `from .pretty import is_expandable as _is_expandable`. Although sys.modules caches the module, the import machinery (attribute binding) still runs every call, a needless per-item cost compared to the previous single module-level import. This is a performance regression, not a correctness error.

findings.summary: The regex [^a-z0-9]+ treats all non-ASCII letters/digits as separators, silently deleting them instead of preserving alphanumeric content.
findings.failure_scenario: slugify("Über Café") returns "ber-caf" (the ü and é are dropped as separators), and slugify("日本語") returns "" — an empty slug. The docstring says non-alphanumerics are replaced, but Unicode letters that ARE alphanumeric per str.isalnum() are discarded, corrupting or emptying slugs for any non-ASCII input.

findings.summary: slugify assumes a string input; passing None or a non-str raises AttributeError instead of handling gracefully.
findings.failure_scenario: slugify(None) raises AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'strip'. A caller mapping over optional/DB-null title fields would crash rather than producing an empty slug.

findings.summary: Using identity comparison `value is not math.inf` instead of `math.isinf(value)` rejects legitimate infinite float values that are not the exact `math.inf` object.
findings.failure_scenario: In CPython each infinite float is a distinct object, so `float('inf') is math.inf` is False. Calling `CapacityLimiterAdapter(float('inf'))` (or setting `adapter.total_tokens = float('inf')`) — a value that is semantically identical to `math.inf` and was accepted before the change and is still accepted by the real backend limiter (which uses `math.isinf`, see _asyncio.py:2047) — now incorrectly raises `TypeError("total_tokens must be an int or math.inf")`. This breaks the documented contract that any int or infinity is allowed and makes the adapter inconsistent with the backend limiter.

findings.summary: Passing `-math.inf` now raises TypeError instead of the previous/expected ValueError, because negative infinity fails the identity check before the `value < 0` branch can run.
findings.failure_scenario: Previously, `total_tokens = -math.inf` passed the `math.isinf` type check and then hit `elif value < 0` producing `ValueError("total_tokens must be >= 0")`. With the identity check `value is not math.inf`, `-math.inf is not math.inf` is True, so it raises `TypeError("total_tokens must be an int or math.inf")` instead, changing the error type for a negative-value input and diverging from the backend limiter behavior.

findings.summary: The memoization cache is keyed only on `point`, ignoring `scale`, so calls with the same point but a different scale return the stale cached result.
findings.failure_scenario: scaled_distance((1,2), 10) caches 30 under key (1,2). A later call scaled_distance((1,2), 100) finds (1,2) already in _cache and returns 30 instead of the correct 300. The cache key must include scale (e.g. (point, scale)).

findings.summary: The module-level `_cache` grows without bound, so long-running processes calling scaled_distance with many distinct points leak memory.
findings.failure_scenario: A process that repeatedly calls scaled_distance with fresh point tuples (e.g. streaming coordinates) accumulates one entry per unique point forever, since nothing evicts entries; memory usage grows unbounded.

findings.summary: update_email writes to the database but does not invalidate/update the read-through cache, so get_user returns stale data.
findings.failure_scenario: Call get_user(1) -> caches {"email": "old@x.com"}. Then call update_email(1, "new@x.com") which updates the DB but leaves _cache[1] unchanged. A subsequent get_user(1) sees user_id still in _cache and returns the stale "old@x.com" instead of "new@x.com". The fix is to del self._cache[user_id] (or update it) inside update_email.

findings.summary: Optional arguments whose type already brackets its metavar (Choice, DateTime) now get wrapped in a second pair of brackets, producing doubled brackets like [[a|b|c]].
findings.failure_scenario: Define a non-required argument with type=click.Choice(["a","b","c"]) (or click.DateTime). Choice.get_metavar returns "[a|b|c]" for a non-required argument (types.py:384). Because make_metavar no longer checks already_bracketed, `if not self.required` wraps it again into "[[a|b|c]]". The help/usage text then shows doubled square brackets instead of "[a|b|c]".

findings.summary: Mutable default argument `batch=[]` is shared across all calls, so it does not start a fresh batch as documented.
findings.failure_scenario: The default list is evaluated once at function-definition time and reused. Call `add_to_batch("a")` returns `["a"]`; a later call `add_to_batch("b")` with no batch argument returns `["a", "b"]` instead of the expected `["b"]`, since state leaks between independent calls. The docstring's promise to "start a new one" is violated. Fix: use `batch=None` and create `batch = []` inside the function when None.

findings.summary: add_bid appends to self.bids without preserving the descending-sorted invariant maintained by __init__, so best_bid() may no longer return the highest bid.
findings.failure_scenario: Book([10, 8]) stores bids = [10, 8]. Calling add_bid(12) yields bids = [10, 8, 12]. best_bid() returns bids[0] == 10 instead of the true highest bid 12, and spread_to(ask) is computed against the wrong best bid (e.g. spread_to(15) returns 5 instead of 3). The fix should insert in sorted order (or re-sort), e.g. bisect.insort into a descending list.

findings.summary: compute_discount includes all line items in the discount base, ignoring each item's "type", so non-discountable items (e.g. gift cards) are discounted.
findings.failure_scenario: Given line_items = [{"price": 5000, "type": "gift_card"}], the coupon discount is computed as min(5000*1000//10000, 2000) = 500 cents even though gift cards typically should not be discounted. The "type" field is documented as present on each item but never consulted when building `base`.

findings.summary: If MAX_ATTEMPTS is <= 0, the loop never runs and `raise last_error` raises None, producing a confusing TypeError instead of a fetch error.
findings.failure_scenario: If MAX_ATTEMPTS is ever set to 0 (or negative) — e.g. via a future config change — `fetch_with_retry` skips the loop entirely, `last_error` stays None, and `raise last_error` triggers `TypeError: exceptions must derive from BaseException` rather than any meaningful fetch failure. There is no guard asserting MAX_ATTEMPTS >= 1.

findings.summary: The grade scale omits the "D" band, so scores 60-69 are graded "F" instead of the conventional "D".
findings.failure_scenario: letter_grade(65) returns "F". On the standard 10-point scale, 60-69 should map to "D"; the function jumps directly from "C" (>=70) to "F", incorrectly failing students in the 60-69 range.

findings.summary: Narrowing except BaseException to except Exception in Client.send leaks the response/connection when a KeyboardInterrupt or other non-Exception BaseException is raised during response.read().
findings.failure_scenario: A user presses Ctrl+C (KeyboardInterrupt) or SystemExit is raised while `response.read()` runs at line 899. Because KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit derive from BaseException but not Exception, the `except Exception` handler no longer runs, so `response.close()` is skipped and the underlying connection is never returned/closed, leaking it from the pool.

findings.summary: Client._send_handling_auth no longer closes the response on non-Exception BaseException (e.g. KeyboardInterrupt) raised during auth-flow read.
findings.failure_scenario: During an auth flow, if a KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit is raised in `auth_flow.send(response)` or `response.read()` (lines 926-931), the `except Exception` handler is skipped, so `response.close()` never runs and the connection leaks.

findings.summary: Client._send_handling_redirects no longer closes the response on non-Exception BaseException raised during redirect handling.
findings.failure_scenario: While following redirects, a KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit raised in a response hook or `response.read()` (lines 958-969) bypasses the `except Exception` handler, so `response.close()` is skipped and the connection leaks.

findings.summary: AsyncClient.send no longer closes the response on asyncio.CancelledError (a BaseException, not Exception) raised during await response.aread(), leaking the connection.
findings.failure_scenario: An async task running AsyncClient.send is cancelled while `await response.aread()` is in progress (line 1603). asyncio.CancelledError derives from BaseException (Python 3.8+), so the `except Exception` handler does not run, `await response.aclose()` is skipped, and the connection is never released back to the pool — leading to pool exhaustion/hangs.

findings.summary: AsyncClient._send_handling_auth no longer closes the response on asyncio.CancelledError during the async auth-flow read.
findings.failure_scenario: During an async auth flow, task cancellation while awaiting `auth_flow.asend(response)` or `response.aread()` (lines 1630-1635) raises CancelledError (BaseException), which is not caught by `except Exception`, so `await response.aclose()` is skipped and the connection leaks.

findings.summary: AsyncClient._send_handling_redirects no longer closes the response on asyncio.CancelledError during async redirect handling.
findings.failure_scenario: While following redirects asynchronously, task cancellation during a response hook or `await response.aread()` (lines 1662-1674) raises CancelledError (BaseException), which bypasses the `except Exception` handler, so `await response.aclose()` is skipped and the connection leaks from the pool.

findings.summary: platform_fee always truncates toward zero (floor for positives), silently rounding fractional cents down rather than to nearest cent.
findings.failure_scenario: For subtotal=199 cents, 199*250//10000 = 49750//10000 = 4 cents, whereas the true fee 4.9750 rounds to 5 cents. Every order whose fee has a fractional part >= 0.5 cent is under-charged by one cent, systematically losing platform revenue. If round-to-nearest was intended this is a bug.

findings.summary: Floor division with a negative subtotal rounds toward negative infinity, producing a fee more negative than expected.
findings.failure_scenario: If a refund/adjustment passes subtotal=-199, then -199*250//10000 = -49750//10000 = -5 (not -4), so the refunded fee is larger in magnitude than the corresponding positive-order fee of 4, breaking symmetry between charges and refunds.

findings.summary: link_id built by concatenating the counter and hash(meta) without a separator can collide for distinct styles, causing distinct terminal hyperlinks to be treated as one.
findings.failure_scenario: Two meta styles get link_ids f"{next(_id_generator)}{hash(meta)}": e.g. id=1,hash=23 -> "123" and id=12,hash=3 -> "123". Two different Style/meta objects then emit the same OSC-8 id ("\x1b]8;id=123;..."), so a terminal groups the two unrelated hyperlinks (shared hover highlighting / activation). This ambiguity is present in this diff's expressions at lines 201 and 252 and was retained from the prior randint-based code.

findings.summary: rank() sorts only by -score and never uses 'id', so items with equal scores are not deterministically tie-broken.
findings.failure_scenario: Given items=[{"score":5,"id":2},{"score":5,"id":1}], the docstring highlights an 'id' field implying id should break ties (e.g. ascending id → id 1 first). Because the key is only -score, Python's stable sort keeps input order, returning id 2 before id 1. Any caller reordering or re-querying items (e.g. different DB row order) then gets a different, non-reproducible ranking for equal-score items.

findings.summary: in_window treats both bounds as inclusive, so adjacent windows overlap at the shared boundary.
findings.failure_scenario: Time windows are conventionally half-open [start, end). With `start <= ts <= end`, two adjacent windows [0,10] and [10,20] both return True for ts=10, double-counting the boundary timestamp. If the intended semantics are half-open, the end comparison should be `ts < end`.

findings.summary: in_window does not guard against an inverted window where start > end, silently returning False for all timestamps.
findings.failure_scenario: If a caller accidentally passes start=20, end=10, the expression `20 <= ts <= 10` is False for every ts, so the empty result is returned with no error, masking the caller's mistake instead of raising.

findings.summary: Tax is computed on the full pre-discount subtotal, then the coupon is applied afterward, so tax is charged on the discounted portion too.
findings.failure_scenario: With base=10_000 cents, TAX_BPS=800, coupon_bps=5000: taxed = 10000 + 800 = 10800; result = 10800 - 5400 = 5400. Standard practice (discount before tax) gives 5000 discounted base, tax 400, total 5400 — but the tax the customer effectively pays here (800*0.5=400 on the discounted-away half) overcharges tax. The customer is taxed on amounts they never paid because of the coupon, inflating the total versus a discount-before-tax computation.

findings.summary: No bounds check on coupon_bps, so a value above 10_000 yields a negative order total.
findings.failure_scenario: order_total(items, coupon_bps=12000) with base=10_000 gives taxed=10800 and returns 10800 - 12960 = -2160 cents, a negative total that downstream billing code would treat as a payout/credit rather than rejecting the invalid coupon.

findings.summary: service_fee uses Python's round(), which does banker's rounding (round-half-to-even), so exact-half fees are rounded down instead of up.
findings.failure_scenario: service_fee(150): 150*300/10000 = 4.5 exactly. round(4.5) returns 4 (round-half-to-even), but the expected 3% fee is 5 cents (half rounds up). Similarly service_fee(350)=10.5 returns 10 instead of 11. This systematically under-charges on half-cent boundaries where the integer part is even.

findings.summary: service_fee performs float division on money (integer cents), risking binary floating-point representation errors that can tip round() the wrong way.
findings.failure_scenario: Because amount*FEE_BPS/10_000 is evaluated in float, values that are mathematically x.5 or exact integers may be stored as x.4999999... or x.5000001..., causing round() to produce an off-by-one cent for certain large or awkward amounts. Integer arithmetic like (amount*FEE_BPS + 5000)//10_000 would avoid this; the current code is not exact for money.

findings.summary: median does not average the two middle values for even-length input, contradicting its docstring.
findings.failure_scenario: median([1, 2, 3, 4]) returns s[4//2] = s[2] = 3 instead of the documented (2+3)/2 = 2.5. Any even-length list yields the upper-middle element rather than the mean of the two central values.

findings.summary: percentile raises IndexError for p=100 because the computed index equals len(s).
findings.failure_scenario: percentile([1,2,3,4], 100) computes int(4*100/100) = 4 and evaluates s[4], which is out of range for a length-4 list, raising IndexError instead of returning the maximum (4).

findings.summary: moving_average drops the final window due to an off-by-one in range(len(xs) - k).
findings.failure_scenario: moving_average([1,2,3,4], 2) iterates i in range(2) = [0,1], producing only [1.5, 2.5] and omitting the last window sum([3,4])/2 = 3.5; there should be len(xs)-k+1 = 3 windows. Additionally, when k == len(xs) it returns [] instead of one average.

findings.summary: mean raises ZeroDivisionError on an empty input list.
findings.failure_scenario: mean([]) computes sum([]) / len([]) = 0 / 0, raising ZeroDivisionError rather than handling the empty case gracefully.

findings.summary: subtotal iterates range(len(items) - 1), skipping the last line item.
findings.failure_scenario: For items=[{"price":100,"qty":1},{"price":200,"qty":1}], the loop runs only for i=0 and returns 100 instead of 300; the final line item is always omitted, and a single-item list returns 0.

findings.summary: mean_line_value divides by len(items) with no guard, raising ZeroDivisionError on empty input.
findings.failure_scenario: mean_line_value([]) computes subtotal([]) // len([]) = 0 // 0, raising ZeroDivisionError instead of returning 0 or handling the empty case.

findings.summary: mean_line_value inherits subtotal's off-by-one, so the average is computed from a sum that omits the last item.
findings.failure_scenario: For two items each worth 100, subtotal returns 100 (last item dropped), so mean_line_value returns 100//2 = 50 instead of the correct 100.

findings.summary: allocate_tax divides by sum(weights) with no guard, raising ZeroDivisionError when weights is empty or all zero.
findings.failure_scenario: allocate_tax(100, []) or allocate_tax(100, [0, 0]) makes total = 0 and evaluates tax_cents * w / 0, raising ZeroDivisionError.

findings.summary: allocate_tax rounds each share independently, so the allocated cents need not sum to tax_cents.
findings.failure_scenario: allocate_tax(10, [1, 1, 1]) yields [round(3.33), round(3.33), round(3.33)] = [3, 3, 3] = 9, losing a cent; conversely other weight splits can over-allocate. Tax allocation should conserve the total.

findings.summary: late_fee returns a negative fee for negative days_late instead of clamping to zero.
findings.failure_scenario: late_fee(-2) returns -1000, producing a negative "fee" (credit) for an order that is not overdue rather than 0.

findings.summary: can_refund's operator precedence makes any cancelled order refundable regardless of paid/shipped state, which may not be intended.
findings.failure_scenario: Python evaluates (paid and not shipped) or cancelled. For order {"paid": False, "shipped": True, "cancelled": True} it returns True, refunding an unpaid, already-shipped order simply because cancelled is True. If the intended rule was paid and (not shipped or cancelled), this returns the wrong answer.

findings.summary: Changing `alias is not None` to truthiness check `alias` skips type validation for falsy-but-invalid alias values.
findings.failure_scenario: With `AliasGenerator(alias=lambda f: 0)` (or any generator returning a falsy value of a wrong type such as `0`, `0.0`, `[]`, `()`), the previous code `if alias is not None and not isinstance(alias, allowed_types)` raised a TypeError. After the change `if alias and not isinstance(...)`, the falsy invalid value bypasses the check entirely and is returned as the alias. In _fields.py it is then assigned to field_info.alias (e.g. an int 0), producing an invalid alias instead of the expected TypeError, leading to downstream errors or incorrect field aliasing.

findings.summary: InvalidSchema docstring now references a non-existent file "defaults.py" and no longer describes what the exception means.
findings.failure_scenario: A developer reading help(InvalidSchema) or the rendered API docs sees "See defaults.py for valid schemas." but there is no requests/defaults.py in the package (confirmed by listing files), so the pointer is dead and the previous meaningful description ("The URL scheme provided is either invalid or unsupported.") is lost.

findings.summary: User-facing error message changed from correct URL terminology "No scheme supplied" to incorrect "No schema supplied".
findings.failure_scenario: Calling requests.get("example.com/path") (no scheme) raises MissingSchema with message "Invalid URL 'example.com/path': No schema supplied. Perhaps you meant http://example.com/path?". "schema" is the wrong term for the URL component (RFC 3986 calls it "scheme"); it is confusing to users and breaks any downstream tooling/tests that grep for the long-standing "No scheme supplied" text.

findings.summary: MissingSchema docstring uses incorrect terminology "schema" instead of the correct URL term "scheme".
findings.failure_scenario: Documentation now reads "The URL schema (e.g. http or https) is missing." The component http/https is a URL "scheme" per RFC 3986, not a "schema"; this misleads readers of the exception's docstring/API docs.

findings.summary: total_pnl iterates range(len(candles) - 1), skipping the last candle and undercounting the sum.
findings.failure_scenario: For candles=[{"pnl": 1.0}, {"pnl": 2.0}, {"pnl": 3.0}], the loop runs i in range(2) = 0,1 and sums only 1.0 + 2.0 = 3.0, omitting the final 3.0. Correct total is 6.0. With a single candle [{"pnl": 5.0}], range(0) is empty and it returns 0.0 instead of 5.0. The last candle's PnL is always dropped.

findings.summary: search_insert sets lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1, causing a non-terminating (infinite) loop when the target is greater than an element.
findings.failure_scenario: Call search_insert([1, 3], 5). Iteration: lo=0, hi=2, mid=1, arr[1]=3<5 so lo=1. Next: lo=1, hi=2, mid=(1+2)//2=1, arr[1]=3<5 so lo=1 again — mid never advances past lo, so lo stays 1 forever and the while loop never terminates. Because mid uses floor division, whenever the binary search narrows to lo and hi=lo+1 with arr[lo]<target, mid equals lo and lo=mid makes no progress. This hangs for any target larger than some element at the search boundary (e.g. searching for a value that should be inserted at the end, or any value exceeding the last element).

findings.summary: Switching to str.splitlines() breaks carriage-return overwrite handling, rendering CR-containing terminal output as multiple lines and making decode_line's \r logic dead code.
findings.failure_scenario: Text.from_ansi("Progress: 50%\rProgress: 100%"): the old code split only on "\n", passed the whole line to decode_line which does line.rsplit("\r",1)[-1] to emulate cursor return, yielding a single line "Progress: 100%". splitlines() now splits on "\r" too, producing two lines ["Progress: 50%", "Progress: 100%"] -> "Progress: 50%\nProgress: 100%". The overwrite semantics are lost and decode_line's rsplit("\r",1) never fires because splitlines already removed all "\r".

findings.summary: str.splitlines() treats many extra control/Unicode characters (\v, \f, \x1c-\x1e, \x85, \u2028, \u2029) as line boundaries, so those bytes in terminal output are now silently dropped and split into new lines.
findings.failure_scenario: Text.from_ansi("a\x85b") or content containing a form feed "a\x0cb": the old re.split(r"(?<=\n)", ...) only broke on "\n", producing a single line "a\x85b"/"a\x0cb". splitlines() breaks on U+0085 (NEL), U+2028, U+2029, \v, \f, and the ASCII file/group/record separators, yielding two lines ["a","b"] and discarding the separator character, changing rendered output.

findings.summary: A trailing newline no longer produces a trailing empty line, dropping the final blank line that the previous implementation emitted.
findings.failure_scenario:
decode("foo
"): old code re.split(r"(?<=
)", "foo
") -> ["foo
", ""] -> after rstrip -> yields Text("foo") and Text(""), so Text.from_ansi joins to "foo
". splitlines() gives ["foo"], yielding only Text("foo") -> "foo". The trailing newline/blank line is lost, changing line counts for callers that rely on it.

findings.summary: Docstring now documents a parameter named `lines (Iterable[str])` that does not exist; the actual parameter is `terminal_text` of type str.
findings.failure_scenario: The decode() signature is `def decode(self, terminal_text: str)`, but the updated Args section describes `lines (Iterable[str]): An iterable of lines...`. Anyone reading the docs/tooling (IDE hints, sphinx) sees a wrong parameter name and type, since the function takes a single str, not an iterable of lines.
